name: Vibravox
description: A dataset of French speech captured with body-conduction audio sensors. It contains audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors (two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone) and audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are included.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poiree, Veronique Zimpfer, Eric Bavu
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poiree, and E. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: Creating the Vibravox BCM dataset involved designing pre-amplification and conditioning circuits for each transducer, coding frontend and back-end software for the recording user interface, adapting housings and fixings for some audio sensors to the human body through 3D modeling and printing, and selecting transducer technologies and recording parameters. The recording process consists of four consecutive steps for each participant: speech-clean, where the participant reads sentences sourced from the French Wikipedia for 15 minutes and each utterance generates a new recording with transcriptions retained; speechless-noisy, where for 2 minutes and 24 seconds the subject remains silent but free to move, swallow, and breathe naturally in a noisy environment created from AudioSet samples played in a 56-loudspeaker spatialization sphere; speechless-clean, repeated for 54 seconds in complete silence to record physiological and sensor noises; and speech-noisy, a final 54-second phase with noise samples replayed in the 3D spatializer from in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events. A total of 200 participants contributed, with 188 retained after post-processing.
rai:dataCollectionType: Direct measurement, Experiments, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous 6-channel audio recordings from five body-conduction sensors and one airborne headset microphone recorded with a Zoom F8n at 48 kHz and 32 bits. Text read by participants originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. For noisy subsets, ambient noise samples were sourced largely from AudioSet and from in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events, spatialized with the ambitools library and rendered by a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The textual data from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice was filtered to produce a simplified dataset with a minimum number of textual and phonemic symbols and to minimize pronunciation uncertainty. Proper names were mostly excluded, retaining only common first names, French town or region names, and country names. Utterances containing numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors were removed. Common text normalization operations were applied, such as lowercasing text and removing punctuation except apostrophes. For noisy-condition experiments, the speechless-noisy subset was dynamically mixed with the speech-clean subset to simulate real-world noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel during recording. Post-processing applied three automatic filters to speech-clean utterances to remove obvious deficiencies such as mispronounced sentences, sensor shifts, malfunctions, or unequipped microphones. Indicators were extracted using the whisper-timestamped model to align transcription with waveform and identify vocalizations. Filters retained only samples with PER[j] < 10%, SNR[i,j] > 1.5 dB, and Lspeech50[i,j] > Lsilence50[i]. If a participant's speech-clean subset was not empty, all recordings for speech-noisy, speechless-clean, and speechless-noisy were systematically added. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with 28,471 sentences. If a sample passed all filters, VAD timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; when adjusted timestamps exceeded original boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset was then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. In the speech-clean subset, participants read sentences sourced from the French Wikipedia and the transcriptions were retained. From normalized text, corresponding phonetic transcriptions using the International Phonetic Alphabet were generated with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For some words, the phonemizer produced language switches that were avoided to preserve the minimal French phonetic alphabet, so a phase of manual phonetic transcription was necessary for unrecognized words such as 'algorithme'.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: text phonemizer of the CoML lab
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task, Phoneme Error Rate was computed for each sample using the Levenshtein distance between the phonetic labeled transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. Audio samples where PER[j] > 10% were discarded. The whisper-timestamped model was used to align transcription with the raw waveform and predict word timestamps in speech segments.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model; Whisper; text phonemizer of the CoML lab
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are reported. The dataset also contains speech samples, physiological sounds, and biometric information discussed as potentially including heart rate and breathing. The paper states the dataset is GDPR compliant, informed consent was obtained, and data were anonymized and encrypted during storage and analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors hope the release will drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support the development of robust communication systems for real-world applications. The dataset is discussed as useful for improving communication in noisy environments, developing voice commands, monitoring vital signs including heart rate, and speaker verification applications such as access control and intelligence gathering. The paper also notes potential military and industrial applications and battlefield forensics uses related to biometric information such as heart rate, breathing, emotional states, and life signals.
rai:dataBiases: To increase the representativeness and inclusivity of the dataset, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants. The dataset is split with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test. The paper also notes that some participants' ear canal anatomy did not fit the rigid in-ear microphone properly, and that one-size-fits-all in-ear designs can cause acoustic sealing issues for certain anatomies.
rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference under such conditions. Some data inconsistencies occurred during collection, including mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. The post-processing filters did not catch all cases, for example when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing. The post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences, with the stated objective of ensuring rigorous analysis and fair comparison rather than maximizing overall performance. The paper also reports that EBEN enhancement improved intelligibility metrics and phoneme transcription but had a detrimental impact on speaker verification performance.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and testing deep learning models for speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. The speech-clean subset contains the most data for training. The speech-noisy subset is of particular interest for showcasing noise-resilient capabilities of body-conduction microphones but primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference. To simulate real-world noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference, users can augment speech-clean with speechless-noisy. The speechless-clean subset can be used for tasks such as heart rate tracking, analyzing sensor noise properties, or generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor-inherent noise. The dataset is also discussed as useful for developing robust communication systems, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs.
